Chapter 5: Legal Definitions and the Limits of Personhood
As Kido dug deeper into the investigation, the focus started to shift—from the world of memories and personal stories to the systems that define who we are on paper. Suddenly, everything hinged on legal processes and official records. It’s strange, isn’t it? How much society relies on documents to decide what makes someone a person. In the eyes of the law, you’re not just a name or a face—you’re a collection of documents: a birth certificate, a family registry, a national ID. These are supposed to make things clear, to tie your name to your story. But for Daisuke, the system just didn’t work. The man everyone knew as Daisuke Taniguchi, well, on paper, he was someone else entirely. Untangling his identity wasn’t simple—it turned into this endless maze of bureaucracy. Officials kept asking for paperwork that simply didn’t exist. The legal definition of a person turned out to be so rigid and narrow that it couldn’t keep up with real life. The system wanted clear answers, but there just weren’t any to give. And the people left behind? They were forced to make sense of a world that suddenly seemed upside down. For Kido, this was a wake-up call. He saw firsthand the huge gap between what the law says and how people actually live. The law tries to keep things neat, to put us in tidy categories. But real lives? They’re messy. People change their names, families shift, and sometimes, people reinvent themselves entirely—none of which fits neatly into a form. The limits of the legal system became painfully obvious when it was time to deal with Daisuke’s estate. Without a clear identity, even basic questions—like who should inherit his things, or who could claim his body—were suddenly impossible to answer. His closest friends and loved ones were left hanging, unable to move forward until the paperwork caught up with the truth of his life. Every time Kido spoke with officials, he felt more frustrated. They kept insisting on forms and signatures, treating those who knew Daisuke best like strangers. Memories and shared experiences meant nothing compared to what was—or wasn’t—on file. It was dehumanizing, boiling a whole life down to a few pieces of paper. For Rie, it was even more painful. The man she loved was being erased by a system that just wouldn’t recognize he ever existed. Dealing with the legal aftermath felt like losing him all over again. Both Rie and Kido were forced to face just how flawed these systems really are. Sure, the law can define a person on paper, but it can’t capture the reality of a life lived outside the lines. Their search for truth became more than just a personal journey—it was a challenge to the very systems that shape how we see ourselves, and each other.
